title: JRE 2333 - Protect Our Parks 15
guestBio: Shane Gillis, Mark Normand, and Ari Shaffir are stand-up comics, writers, and podcasters.
tldr: Shane Gillis, Mark Normand, and Ari Shaffir discuss their comedy careers and podcast experiences
The comedians talk about the challenges of stand-up comedy in the modern era
Discussion covers their various podcast projects and comedy writing processes
The group shares stories from touring and performing across the country
Conversation touches on the state of comedy and creative freedom in entertainment
The episode features the natural banter and humor between three working comedians
recap:
JRE 2333 brings together three of comedy's most prolific voices: Shane Gillis, Mark Normand, and Ari Shaffir. This episode is a masterclass in how genuinely funny people just riff when they get together. There's no particular agenda here, just three guys who spend their lives making people laugh sitting down to talk about what that actually entails.

The conversation flows naturally between their various projects. Shane's working on his Netflix series "Tires" with a second season coming June 5, while simultaneously co-hosting "Matt and Shane's Secret Podcast" and running the sketch comedy operation "Gilly and Keeves" with John McKeever. Meanwhile, Mark's juggling the "All Over the Road" podcast, co-hosting "Tuesdays with Stories" with Joe List, and "We Might Be Drunk" with Sam Morril. These aren't side projects either, these are working comedians actually grinding it out daily.

What becomes clear is that modern comedy success requires multiple revenue streams. The touring game is still important, but podcasting, streaming specials, and sketch content are where comedians can actually build sustainable careers. The guys talk about the freedom that comes with platforms they control versus the constraints of traditional media. There's a real honesty about what works and what doesn't in comedy right now.

The episode captures something essential about working comedians: they're obsessed with the craft itself. These guys aren't chasing celebrity or trying to be famous for famous sake. They're talking about what makes people laugh, what kills on stage, how timing works, and why certain material lands. That shop talk between professionals is always more interesting than any prepared bit.

What's also evident is the community aspect of comedy. These three know each other, have worked together, have history. That familiarity breeds a comfort that allows for real conversation rather than performance. Joe clearly enjoys this kind of episode where it's just funny people being funny with each other.
